title: American film since 2012 (two-film study): Joker and Get Out

items.definition: A mentally ill, abused loner is ground down by an uncaring city until he kills: the monster is made, not born.
items.examples: Arthur Fleck loses his job, his medication and his mother, and the “clown” protests turn him into a symbol.
keyFacts: The film makes the spectator uncomfortably sympathise with Arthur: the whole spectatorship game
It blames class neglect and social indifference, which is its ideological argument
Killer line: “Phillips aligns the spectator with Arthur through subjective camerawork and an unreliable narrative, so sympathy curdles into complicity.”
items.examTip: Every Joker paragraph should link a technique to HOW the spectator is positioned.

items.definition: Inequality, austerity and a defunded mental-health system; the clown protests echo Occupy-style anger at the rich.
items.examples: Arthur’s social worker tells him the city has cut funding: “They don’t give a shit about people like you, Arthur.”
keyFacts: Released in 2019, amid debates about wealth inequality and populist anger
Thomas Wayne calls the protesters “clowns”, echoing politicians dismissing the poor
The film was feared to inspire real violence: US cinemas increased security at screenings
items.examTip: Context + spectatorship: different audiences read the riots as protest or as warning.

items.definition: A deliberate homage to Scorsese’s Taxi Driver (1976) and The King of Comedy (1982): lonely men, decaying cities.
items.examples: Robert De Niro, star of both Scorsese films, plays talk-show host Murray Franklin.
keyFacts: Gotham is a rubbish-strewn, strike-bound early-1980s New York
Borrows the New Hollywood character study inside a comic-book franchise
Spectators who know the references read Arthur through Travis Bickle and Rupert Pupkin
items.examTip: Intertextuality is an “auteur cue” and a “genre cue” for spectator response.

items.term: Institutional context: a mainstream studio film
items.definition: A Warner Bros./DC comic-book property made as a gritty, R-rated character study rather than a superhero film.
items.examples: It premiered at Venice in 2019 and won the Golden Lion, the first comic-book film to do so; Oscars followed for Joaquin Phoenix (Best Actor) and Hildur Guðnadóttir (Best Score).
keyFacts: The first R-rated film to gross over $1 billion worldwide (about $1.07 billion)
Mainstream in funding and IP, but art-house in tone: blurs the spec’s mainstream/independent divide
Marketing used the brand to bring mass audiences to a challenging film
items.examTip: Mainstream ≠ simple: a mass audience brings a wider range of readings.

items.definition: Character-locked, often handheld camera and tight framing trap us with Arthur in a sickly green-yellow city.
items.examples: Close-ups of Arthur’s face and body; claustrophobic subway carriages and corridors.
keyFacts: Arthur is in almost every shot: restricted narration aligns us with him
Low-key, sickly lighting and grime connote decay
Later the palette brightens to red and orange as he becomes Joker: his liberation looks seductive
items.examTip: Link camera to alignment: “the camera never leaves Arthur, so the spectator is forced to share his perspective”.

items.definition: A mournful solo cello score, often following Arthur’s movements, pulls the spectator into sympathy.
items.examples: The cello swells after the subway killings as Arthur dances in the bathroom.
keyFacts: Arthur’s involuntary laughter is a recurring sound motif of pain disguised as joy
Needle-drops like “Rock and Roll Part 2” on the stairs make his transformation feel triumphant
Music cues ask for sympathy that the images might make us resist
items.examTip: The sample question asks about “visual and soundtrack cues”: have one sound cue per film ready.

items.term: Mise-en-scène: the stairs and the make-up
items.definition: The long Bronx staircase and the clown make-up chart Arthur’s descent and rebirth.
items.examples: He trudges UP the stairs in grey clothes early on; later he dances DOWN them in a red suit and full Joker make-up.
keyFacts: Make-up = a mask of forced happiness; it runs when he cries
Red suit marks his new identity and power
Cramped flat, TV and fridge show isolation and fantasy
items.examTip: Repeated settings with changed meaning = strong mise-en-scène motif analysis.

items.definition: An extreme physical performance: severe weight loss, a contorted body and a painful, uncontrollable laugh.
items.examples: The bathroom dance after the subway killings was not in the script: it replaced a scene of Arthur talking to himself in the mirror, improvised as Phillips played Guðnadóttir’s score on set.
keyFacts: Phoenix lost 52 pounds for the role and said the hunger brought vulnerability and weakness
The body as a site of suffering makes the spectator wince and sympathise
Phoenix won the Oscar for Best Actor
items.examTip: Performance is a “cue” to spectator response: name a gesture, not just “good acting”.

items.term: Editing and narrative: the unreliable narrator
items.definition: Scenes are replayed to reveal they were imagined, so the spectator can no longer trust what they have seen.
items.examples: Arthur’s romance with his neighbour Sophie is replayed without her: she was never there.
keyFacts: Forces the spectator from passive acceptance to active questioning
Leaves the whole film open: was any of it real?
The final asylum scene may frame everything as fantasy
items.examTip: Your best evidence for “a constant shift between passive and active spectatorship”.

items.definition: Three drunk Wall Street men harass and beat Arthur; he shoots them all.
items.examples: Low-key lighting, flickering carriage lights, claustrophobic framing; afterwards the bathroom dance to the cello.
keyFacts: Spectatorship: guilty relief (passive identification) collides with horror (active judgement)
Ideology: the killings spark the anti-rich clown movement
The first shooting is self-defence; the last is an execution, testing how far we follow him
items.examTip: Strongest single Joker sequence for both specialist areas.

items.definition: Fully transformed, Arthur dances triumphantly down the Bronx steps to a glam-rock anthem.
items.examples: Celebratory camera, slow motion and a bright palette contrast with the earlier trudges up the same steps.
keyFacts: Form celebrates a murderer’s rebirth: seductive and deliberately uncomfortable
Shows how visual and sound cues can make the spectator complicit
The steps became a real tourist site: evidence of the film’s cultural reach
items.examTip: Ask: does the spectator resist this pleasure? That is active spectatorship.

items.term: The Murray Franklin show and the riot
items.definition: Arthur confesses live on TV, rants about society abandoning people like him, shoots Murray, and Gotham riots.
items.examples: Cross-cutting between the studio and burning streets; rioters lift Arthur onto a car bonnet like a messiah.
keyFacts: Ideological climax: neglect produces violence
Preferred reading (sympathy for the abandoned) vs oppositional reading (alarm at glorified violence)
Media spectacle: the TV show turns violence into entertainment
items.examTip: Use Stuart Hall’s readings here to show diverse spectator response.

items.definition: Subjective camera and score invite passive identification; the violence and unreliable narration push active judgement.
items.examples: We feel with Arthur in the subway, then must resist the celebratory stair dance, and split over the Murray Franklin show.
keyFacts: Passive = absorbed, aligned, swept along; active = questioning, resisting, bringing our own values
Murray Smith: we are ALIGNED with Arthur (we see what he sees) without necessarily feeling ALLEGIANCE
The shift is constant: the film keeps rewarding and then punishing sympathy
items.examTip: Make a judgement: “to a significant extent, because the film is designed to make sympathy uncomfortable”.

items.definition: The film argues that inequality, austerity and the indifference of the rich produce violence.
items.examples: Thomas Wayne’s contempt; cut welfare services; Wall Street men on the subway.
keyFacts: Marxist reading: class conflict between Gotham’s rich and poor
Critics debated whether it critiques or glamorises angry, isolated men
Its ideology is ambiguous, which makes spectator response diverse
items.examTip: Evaluate: an ideological reading explains the riots, but the ambiguity limits a single reading.

items.term: Joker: viewing conditions and diverse response
items.definition: Fears of copycat violence, heavy security and online debate shaped how audiences watched the film.
items.examples: Families of victims of the 2012 Aurora cinema shooting wrote to Warner Bros. with concerns before release.
keyFacts: The spec asks about “the impact of different viewing conditions on spectator response”
Cinema crowds, home streaming and repeat viewing all change response
Some viewers identified with Arthur; others read him as a warning
items.examTip: Viewing conditions is a spec point many students forget: one sentence earns credit.

items.definition: A Black photographer meets his white girlfriend’s liberal family, who steal Black bodies: horror as social critique.
items.examples: Dean Armitage: “I would have voted for Obama a third time if I could.”
keyFacts: Attacks covert, liberal racism rather than open hatred
Restricted to Chris’s point of view, so we share his paranoia
Killer line: “Peele weaponises the horror genre to expose liberal racism, positioning a mixed audience to feel the surveillance of the Black body.”
items.examTip: The spec says Get Out “uses the very mainstream genres of Horror and Comedy” to deliver social critique.

items.definition: The “post-racial” myth after Obama; police violence and Black Lives Matter; racism hidden behind liberal smiles.
items.examples: The garden-party auction evokes slavery behind liberal smiles; the opening abduction makes white suburbia the threat.
keyFacts: Written during the Obama years, released weeks after Trump’s inauguration
Fetishisation and commodification of Black bodies echo slavery
“The Sunken Place” entered everyday language as a metaphor
items.examTip: Always connect context to a scene and a technique.

items.definition: Made by Blumhouse on a micro-budget of about $4.5 million, earning about $255 million worldwide.
items.examples: Peele won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay; the film was nominated for Best Picture.
keyFacts: Blumhouse model: low budgets in return for creative control for the director
This let a first-time director make a radical film with full control
Released by Universal: independent production, mainstream distribution
Four Oscar nominations (Picture, Director, Actor for Kaluuya, Original Screenplay); Best Picture went to The Shape of Water
items.examTip: Institutional context explains WHY its ideology could be so pointed.

items.term: Cultural context: Peele and the horror tradition
items.definition: Peele came from sketch comedy and draws on Night of the Living Dead, Rosemary’s Baby and The Stepford Wives.
items.examples: The smiling, controlled suburban wives recall The Stepford Wives (1975).
keyFacts: Comedy timing helps him control tension and release
Black horror tradition: Romero’s Black hero in Night of the Living Dead (1968)
Genre knowledge is a cue: we expect horror tropes and Peele flips them
items.examTip: Genre cues are explicitly named in the spec’s spectatorship content.

items.definition: Toby Oliver’s camera stays tied to Chris, so the spectator shares what he notices and what he misses.
items.examples: Point-of-view shots of Walter sprinting at night and Georgina staring; Chris’s camera flash exposes the truth.
keyFacts: Chris is a photographer: looking and being looked at is the film’s theme
Calm, bright suburban daylight that feels wrong
The phone camera flash breaks the hypnosis: seeing clearly = resistance
items.examTip: “Restricted narration” is the precise term: use it.

items.definition: The teacup and spoon, the deer, the cotton, the silent Black servants: clues hiding in plain sight.
items.examples: Chris pulls stuffing out of the chair and plugs his ears with cotton, picking cotton to free himself.
keyFacts: The deer links to Chris’s guilt over his mother and to hunted Black bodies
Rose’s white milk and separated Froot Loops hint at her nature
A first viewing and a rewatch produce different responses: active spectatorship
items.examTip: Motifs + repeat viewing = an excellent viewing-conditions point.

items.definition: Michael Abels’ score uses Swahili voices warning Chris to listen to his ancestors and run.
items.examples: “Sikiliza Kwa Wahenga” plays over the opening credits; “Run Rabbit Run” plays in the abductor’s car.
keyFacts: Swahili lyrics address Black ancestry and are opaque to many viewers: different audiences, different access
The spoon on china becomes a terrifying sound trigger
Jump-scare stings are genre cues for horror audiences
items.examTip: A sound cue that different audiences understand differently = diverse response.

items.definition: Kaluuya’s restrained, watchful Chris holds back anger, letting small reactions carry the tension.
items.examples: In the Sunken Place a single tear runs down his frozen face.
keyFacts: Kaluuya was nominated for the Best Actor Oscar
Betty Gabriel’s Georgina smiles while crying: a body controlled by someone else
Lil Rel Howery’s Rod gives comic release and voices the audience’s fears
items.examTip: Performance as a cue: name the tear or Georgina’s smile.

items.definition: A Black man walking through a white suburb at night is stalked and bundled into a car.
items.examples: A long take; “Run Rabbit Run” plays from the car; a knight’s helmet hides the attacker.
keyFacts: Flips the horror trope of a white woman alone in a dangerous city
Positions white suburbia as the threat from the first scene
Andre’s line about feeling like “a sore thumb” sets up the theme of being looked at
items.examTip: Strong for genre cues and for ideology together.

items.term: The hypnosis and the Sunken Place
items.definition: Missy stirs a teacup; Chris sinks into a black void, watching the world through a distant screen, paralysed.
items.examples: Subjective camera, slow falling motion, muffled sound, the spoon’s chime.
keyFacts: Peele has described the Sunken Place as a metaphor for the marginalisation of Black people
Restricted POV makes us FEEL the paralysis: deep passive immersion
Chris watches the world on a “screen”: the spectator watching a film
items.examTip: Signature scene: use it for visual AND soundtrack cues.

items.term: The garden party and silent auction
items.definition: White guests inspect Chris’s body; later they bid silently with bingo cards while Dean stands by his portrait.
items.examples: Intercutting the auction with Chris and Rose by the lake: we know before he does.
keyFacts: Evokes a slave auction: commodification of the Black body made literal
Dramatic irony shifts spectators from sharing Chris’s ignorance to knowing more than him
Guests praise Tiger Woods and Black physique: fetishisation disguised as admiration
items.examTip: The ideological heart of the film.

subtopics.title: Spectatorship and ideology in Get Out

items.term: Get Out: passive and active spectatorship
items.definition: Restricted POV immerses us in Chris’s fear; clues, irony and real-world knowledge make us actively read the film.
items.examples: Passive in the Sunken Place; active at the garden-party auction, where we know more than Chris.
keyFacts: Black and white spectators may be positioned differently: some recognise the microaggressions instantly
bell hooks’ “oppositional gaze”: Black spectators looking back critically
The film shifts us constantly between immersion and suspicion
items.examTip: Contrast with Joker: Get Out asks us to identify with the victim, Joker with the perpetrator.

items.term: Get Out: ideology of liberal racism
items.definition: Racism persists behind progressive smiles: white liberals admire, consume and possess Black bodies.
items.examples: Jim Hudson, the blind art dealer, wants Chris’s “eye”: admiration as theft.
keyFacts: Challenges the dominant “post-racial” ideology
The Coagula procedure literalises cultural appropriation
Rose: the girlfriend figure as the ultimate betrayer
items.examTip: Evaluate the ideological approach: it explains the satire, but genre pleasure also matters.

items.term: Get Out: genre and auteur cues
items.definition: Horror conventions set expectations; Peele’s comic timing and planted motifs build his auteur signature.
items.examples: The jump scare of Walter running at Chris; the deer collision as an omen.
keyFacts: Genre cues tell spectators how to feel, then Peele subverts them
Peele’s later films (Us, Nope) confirm motifs: doubles, watching, social horror
Audience knowledge of Peele as a comedian shaped expectations
items.examTip: The spec names narrative, visual, musical, performance, genre and auteur cues: cover two or three.

items.definition: The spectator is absorbed by the film, identifies with characters and accepts the position the film offers.
items.examples: Feeling relief when Arthur shoots the Wall Street men; falling with Chris into the Sunken Place.
keyFacts: Linked to older “effects” and psychoanalytic theories of film
Classical continuity editing and subjective camera encourage it
Never total: spectators always bring something of themselves
items.examTip: Define both passive and active in the introduction of every spectatorship essay.

items.definition: The spectator questions, interprets and resists, bringing their own knowledge, values and context.
items.examples: Resisting the celebration of Arthur’s stair dance; reading the dramatic irony of Get Out’s auction.
keyFacts: David Bordwell: viewers actively build the story from cues (cognitive approach)
Ambiguity, unreliable narrators and irony provoke active viewing
Rewatching makes spectators more active
items.examTip: Exam stem: “a constant shift between passive and active spectatorship”.

items.term: Stuart Hall: preferred, negotiated, oppositional readings
items.definition: Hall’s encoding/decoding model: audiences may accept, partly accept or reject the meaning a text intends.
items.examples: Joker: preferred = sympathy for the abandoned; oppositional = it glamorises violent men.
keyFacts: Preferred: the reading the film encourages
Negotiated: accepted in part, adapted to the viewer’s situation
Oppositional: rejected; aberrant: a reading far from anything intended
items.examTip: The spec lists preferred, negotiated, oppositional and aberrant readings.

items.term: Murray Smith: the structure of sympathy
items.definition: We engage with characters through recognition, alignment (access to their view) and allegiance (moral support).
items.examples: We are aligned with Arthur almost all the time, but allegiance is withdrawn as he kills.
keyFacts: Alignment ≠ allegiance: you can see through someone’s eyes without approving
Explains how films make us “root for” or recoil from characters
From Engaging Characters (1995)
items.examTip: Precise theory that separates you from answers that only say “we sympathise”.

items.definition: Mulvey (1975) argued Classical cinema positions the spectator as male, with women as objects “to-be-looked-at”.
items.examples: Get Out reworks the gaze: white guests looking at Chris’s Black body as an object.
keyFacts: From “Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema”
Psychoanalytic: scopophilia (pleasure in looking) and identification
Criticised for assuming a single, passive spectator
items.examTip: Use the gaze flexibly: who looks, who is looked at, and with what power.

items.definition: hooks argued Black spectators, especially Black women, look back critically and resist dominant images.
items.examples: Black audiences recognising the microaggressions at the Armitage party before Chris names them.
keyFacts: From Black Looks: Race and Representation (1992)
Looking critically is a form of resistance
Shows that spectator identity shapes response
items.examTip: Excellent for “reasons for the uniformity or diversity of response”.

items.definition: Narrative, visual, musical, performance, genre and auteur cues steer how the spectator feels and thinks.
items.examples: The cello (musical), the stairs (visual), Phoenix’s laugh (performance), horror stings (genre), Peele’s motifs (auteur).
keyFacts: Listed directly in the spec’s spectatorship content
Cues can work together or against each other (upbeat music over violence)
Viewing conditions (cinema, phone, crowd, alone) affect how strongly cues work
items.examTip: Sample stem: “visual and soundtrack cues in influencing spectator response”.

items.definition: The values and beliefs a film conveys or is shaped by, which may reinforce or challenge a society’s dominant ideas.
items.examples: Get Out challenges the post-racial myth; Joker argues inequality creates violence.
keyFacts: Dominant ideology = the beliefs presented as “normal” in a society
Films can reinforce, challenge or be contradictory
Spec: connotations of visuals and sounds, binary oppositions, spectator positioning, ideological perspectives
items.examTip: Always say WHICH ideology (Marxist, feminist, anti-racist) you are applying.

items.definition: Marxism reads films through class conflict; Gramsci’s hegemony is how the ruling class makes its values seem natural.
items.examples: Joker: Wayne’s wealth vs Arthur’s poverty; Shaun of the Dead: workers as zombies.
keyFacts: Althusser: institutions (media, school, family) reproduce ideology
Films can expose hegemony or quietly support it
Useful for Joker, Trainspotting and Shaun
items.examTip: Name the theorist briefly, then get straight to the film evidence.

items.definition: Ideological criticism reveals hidden values but can ignore pleasure, genre, authorship and audience diversity.
items.examples: Reading Get Out only as ideology misses its effectiveness as a scary, funny horror film.
keyFacts: The spec requires “an evaluation of the ideological critical approach to film”
Strength: explains why films matter politically
Weakness: risks one fixed meaning; spectators read differently
items.examTip: Put at least one evaluative sentence in every paragraph for AO2.
